introduction: This foundational level establishes the parameters of homogeneous liquid mixtures. It introduces Henry's Law governing gas-in-liquid solubility, Raoult's Law for ideal binary liquid mixtures, and defines the four core Colligative Properties that depend strictly on particle count, not identity.

core_concepts.title: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
core_concepts.description: The solubility of a gas in a liquid at a constant temperature is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid surface. Mathematically, $p = K_H \cdot x$, where $p$ is the partial pressure of the gaseous solute, $x$ is its mole fraction in the solution, and $K_H$ is the Henry's Law constant. Crucially, $K_H$ increases as temperature increases, which explains why gases are less soluble in hot liquids (e.g., aquatic life is more comfortable in cold water).

core_concepts.title: Vapor Pressure and Raoult's Law
core_concepts.description: Vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by vapors in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid phase at a given temperature. For a volatile binary solution of two liquids A and B, Raoult's Law states that the partial vapor pressure of each component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in solution: $p_A = p_A^\circ x_A$ and $p_B = p_B^\circ x_B$. The total vapor pressure is $P_{\text{total}} = p_A + p_B = p_A^\circ x_A + p_B^\circ x_B$.

core_concepts.title: Ideal Solutions
core_concepts.description: Solutions that obey Raoult's Law perfectly across the entire concentration range. This occurs when the molecular interactions between components ($A-B$) are identical to those in the pure liquids ($A-A$ and $B-B$). Thermodynamic criteria: $\Delta V_{\text{mixing}} = 0$, $\Delta H_{\text{mixing}} = 0$, $\Delta S_{\text{mixing}} > 0$, and $\Delta G_{\text{mixing}} < 0$. Examples: n-hexane + n-heptane, Benzene + Toluene.

core_concepts.title: Introduction to Colligative Properties
core_concepts.description:
Properties of dilute solutions that depend strictly on the total number of solute particles (concentration) present in the solution, completely independent of the nature or identity of the solute. There are four distinct colligative properties: 
1. Relative Lowering of Vapor Pressure (RLVP)
2. Elevation of Boiling Point
3. Depression of Freezing Point
4. Osmotic Pressure

important_entities.name: Universal Liquid State Criteria
important_entities.key_fact: For any dissolution process to occur spontaneously, $\Delta G_{\text{mixing}}$ must be negative and $\Delta S_{\text{mixing}}$ must be positive.
important_entities.significance: Even in highly non-ideal solutions where heat is absorbed (endothermic, $\Delta H > 0$), a solution can still form if the randomness increase ($T\Delta S$) overrides the enthalpy barrier, keeping $\Delta G$ negative.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In competitive exams, you will be given a table of $K_H$ values for different gases and asked which gas is the most soluble. Remember: $x = p / K_H$. Therefore, at a constant pressure, a HIGHER $K_H$ value mathematically corresponds to a LOWER solubility. Do not associate a large constant with high solubility!

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Ideal means No Change except Chaos
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: For an ideal solution, everything structural remains unperturbed: no change in volume ($\Delta V=0$), no heat evolved or absorbed ($\Delta H=0$). The only driving forces are basic thermodynamics: chaos increases ($\Delta S > 0$) and the process happens on its own ($\Delta G < 0$).

exam_strategy_tips: When calculating the vapor pressure of a mixture using $P_{\text{total}} = p_A^\circ x_A + p_B^\circ x_B$, make sure that $x_A$ and $x_B$ are the mole fractions in the LIQUID phase. If the question asks for the mole fraction of a component in the VAPOR phase ($y_A$), use Dalton's Law: $y_A = p_A / P_{\text{total}} = p_A^\circ x_A / P_{\text{total}}$.
